title: What Makes a Man? (Toxic Masculinity & Male Power Fantasy in Grappler Baki)
summary: A long philosophical essay using Grappler Baki as modern mythology to define masculinity. NH rejects the toxic/healthy split, arguing masculinity is both Apollonian and Dionysian, that its 'original' form must be refined by culture and morality and put to the service of protecting others, and that strength, purpose, self-actualization and male competition are its core.
claims: Male power fantasies, stories with characters men want to resemble for their masculine traits, have always existed from Greek and Norse myth to manga and are healthy because they give men a blueprint
Masculinity should not be split into good and bad; it contains both Apollonian (order, civilization) and Dionysian (chaos, violence) traits and every male trait has a role
Young men idolize 'literally me' villains like Patrick Bateman because those characters express masculinity without shame, a catharsis for men restricted their whole lives
The less masculinity in a society, the more young men gravitate to hypermasculine online caricatures who are only playing a role
Yujiro in Baki is the caricature of toxic hypermasculinity and is coded as what not to be; Baki is written as his opposite
We live in a fatherless society: many young men have no masculine role models, or fathers who themselves do not know how to be men
Men do not build strength just for their ego; in Baki as in life they fight for the people in their lives, mostly women
Women are the driving force behind much of what men do; without them consumerism would largely vanish
Masculinity is both shield and sword; reducing the sword to cut harm also reduces the protection women and society benefit from
The only way to contain toxic masculinity is with more masculinity: only strength can oppose strength
He proposes renaming toxic masculinity 'original masculinity': undiscriminated aggression aimed at domination, natural but not therefore good
Healthy masculinity is original masculinity refined by culture and morality and put at the service of the weak; protecting still requires aggression
Whether violence is toxic or heroic is largely a matter of perspective, as with Aragorn from the orcs' point of view; strength is always at the heart of masculinity
Regard with suspicion anyone trying to make you weaker or promoting a philosophy of passivity
Pursue strength but know why; without a why you end up with strength you have no use for, as Baki did
Copying hypermasculine role models makes young men lose their identity; you will never become them, and if you did you would be a monster
Anyone selling you how to be a man is a scam artist; masculinity is a personal quest of self-actualization unique to each individual
Becoming a man does not kill the boy inside; keeping some boyishness without clinging to it makes for a happier life and a better role model
Being a man includes the full range of emotions, crying, grief and joy, not just anger and stoicism; the strongest people are the kindest
Jack Hanma represents the fear of weakness; many men take steroids out of that fear, deluding themselves that it will make them men
Motobe represents the fear of aging, since aging means losing strength and agency as a man
The Baki author, a martial artist and lifter, said the story was meant as a modern mythology for Japanese men he saw as lacking masculinity; Toriyama similarly coded Goku as an Asian Superman
A man is not born, he is made: masculinity needs culture to flourish, whereas femininity comes more naturally
Self-actualization requires some solitude, but the lone-wolf grind myth is false; a man's biggest breakthroughs come in the presence of other men
Competition is not me against you but both getting better; sport is a microcosm of male competition that creates suffering but also progress
He loves natural bodybuilding because the community shares mistakes and knowledge to make the next generation's lives easier
Like a male lion guarding the pride, masculinity looks useless when it is doing its job because nothing happens; this invisibility leads societies to dismiss it
